title: CAN A MAN MARRY HIS DEAD BROTHER’S WIFE?
paragraphs:
CAN A MAN MARRY HIS DEAD BROTHER’S WIFE?
The Strange Duty Behind Levirate Marriage—and the Stunning Gospel Truth Hidden Behind the Sandal, the Widow, and the Name That Must Not Disappear
Imagine standing at your brother’s funeral.
The dust settles.
The mourners eventually leave.
His widow remains.
Then someone opens the Law of Moses and tells you something that sounds almost unbelievable to modern ears:
Under certain circumstances, you may now have a responsibility toward the woman who had been your brother’s wife.
Not merely to give her money.
Not merely to check on her.
Marriage.
And suddenly one of the strangest passages in the Old Testament becomes intensely personal.
Would God really command something like that?
Was a woman simply “passed” from one brother to another?
Does this contradict biblical prohibitions concerning a brother’s wife?
And why, centuries later, would people confront Jesus Christ Himself with a bizarre story about one woman marrying seven brothers?
There is more happening here than an obscure ancient marriage custom.
Much more.
Because underneath the widow, the dead brother, the family name, the elders at the gate, and even the removed sandal is a theme that runs like a scarlet thread through Scripture:
A person is gone.
A household is in danger of disappearing.
Someone vulnerable is left behind.
And another person is called to bear a cost so that what seemed destined for death does not simply vanish.
That is where this story begins.
And before it ends, it will take us somewhere far greater than ancient Israel.
It will take us to Jesus.
The passage at the center of the question is Deuteronomy 25:5–10.
The Hebrew begins:
“כִּי־יֵשְׁבוּ אַחִים יַחְדָּו”
Ki-yeshvu achim yachdav...
“When brothers dwell together...”
Then comes the tragedy.
One brother dies.
And critically, he dies without the offspring contemplated by the law.

His widow is now in an extremely vulnerable position within the social and economic realities of the ancient world, while the deceased man’s family line and inheritance are also threatened with extinction.
The Torah therefore describes an extraordinary family obligation.
The Hebrew says:
“יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ וּלְקָחָהּ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וְיִבְּמָהּ”
Yevamah yavo aleha, uleqachah lo le’ishah, veyibbemah.
Her husband’s brother was to take her as his wife and perform the duty of a husband’s brother.
That last word matters.
Veyibbemah.
It comes from the Hebrew family of words associated with yibbum—what English readers commonly call “levirate marriage.”
“Levirate,” incidentally, does not come from the tribe of Levi. It comes through Latin levir, meaning a husband’s brother.
The biblical concept is very specific.
This was not permission for an Israelite man to look at his brother’s widow and say, “My brother is dead, therefore she belongs to me.”
Nothing remotely that casual is happening.
The law addresses a particular covenantal and familial crisis.
A man has died without the heir envisioned in the passage.
His household is facing erasure.
His widow faces an uncertain future.
His name could disappear from his place within Israel.
And so Deuteronomy explains the purpose:
The offspring would continue the deceased brother’s name so that his name would not be “blotted out” from Israel.
That sentence changes the entire emotional atmosphere of the passage.
This was not primarily a law about male appetite.
It was about responsibility.
Family continuity.
Inheritance.
The preservation of a dead brother’s household.
And provision within a covenant community.
In other words, the surviving brother was not being handed a prize.
He was being handed an obligation.
There is a world of difference.
And Scripture makes that painfully obvious because the man could refuse.
But refusal was not treated as though nothing had happened.
The widow could go publicly to the elders.
The man would be summoned.
If he persisted in refusing, she removed his sandal and performed the prescribed act of public reproach.
Why a sandal?

In the biblical world, sandals could carry legal symbolism connected with property and transactions. Ruth 4 gives us another striking scene involving redemption, family inheritance, and the removal of a sandal.
The image is almost impossible to forget.
A man stands before the community...
with one sandal removed...
because he would not “build up his brother’s house.”
That phrase is devastating.
Because the issue was bigger than romance.
Someone else’s house was collapsing.
The question was whether a relative would accept the cost of helping preserve it.
And suddenly the strange law begins to feel less strange.
Because every generation understands this question:
What do you do when loving someone costs you something?
What happens when responsibility arrives disguised as inconvenience?
What happens when doing what is right interferes with the life you had planned?
We love redemption when we are the ones being rescued.
We struggle with redemption when we are the ones expected to pay a price.
And Scripture refuses to let us romanticize that tension.
Consider the painful story of Judah and Tamar in Genesis 38, which predates the codified Deuteronomic legislation but contains related family-duty concerns.
Judah’s son Er dies.
Then Onan is expected to fulfill responsibility toward Tamar.
But Onan realizes something.
The resulting offspring would not simply advance his own interests.
So he wants the sexual benefit while deliberately frustrating the family obligation.
That is one reason the story is so often misunderstood when ripped from its context.
The central scandal is profoundly connected to selfishness and refusal of covenant responsibility.
Onan wants something from Tamar.
He does not want to give what responsibility requires of him.
And God sees it.
That should make every Christian uncomfortable in the best possible way.
Because sometimes our greatest spiritual problem is not that we refuse God completely.
Sometimes we want the benefits of belonging to God while resisting the responsibilities of belonging to God.
We want forgiveness without repentance.
Comfort without obedience.
Grace without transformation.
A Savior without a Lord.
Heaven without surrender.
We want Jesus to rescue our house while we remain unwilling to inconvenience ourselves for anybody else’s.
Then comes Ruth.
A widow.
A family devastated by death.
An uncertain future.
A field.
A relative.
A legal proceeding at the city gate.
A sandal.
And a man named Boaz.

Ruth’s story intersects with Israel’s broader laws and customs concerning family redemption and preservation, though the situation in Ruth should not simply be flattened into an identical case of Deuteronomy 25.
That distinction matters.
Boaz is not Ruth’s deceased husband’s literal brother.
Ruth intertwines themes of kinship, property redemption, family continuation, and marriage in its own particular circumstances.
Yet the theological beauty is unmistakable.
Ruth begins surrounded by graves.
Her husband is dead.
Her future looks empty.
Naomi herself speaks as a woman who feels emptied by suffering.
Then redemption enters the story.
And notice what biblical redemption looks like.
It costs somebody something.
Boaz does not merely feel sorry for Ruth.
He acts.
He assumes responsibility.
He publicly commits himself.
He pays the cost associated with redemption.
And through that apparently small family drama, God is moving history toward something neither Ruth nor Boaz could possibly see in full.
A family line continues.
Generations pass.
David comes.
And eventually...
Jesus Christ.
Do not rush past that.
A grieving Moabite widow who could easily have disappeared into ancient history becomes part of the genealogy through which Matthew introduces the Messiah.
God took widowhood.
Death.
Loss.
Family complications.
Cultural scandal.
And human vulnerability...
and threaded them into the earthly ancestry of Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But now we have to address the question people immediately ask.
Doesn't the Bible elsewhere prohibit taking a brother’s wife?
Yes, Scripture contains such a prohibition.
Leviticus 18:16 forbids uncovering the nakedness of one’s brother’s wife, and Leviticus 20:21 likewise condemns taking a brother’s wife.
So is the Bible contradicting itself?
No.

Deuteronomy 25 describes a defined circumstance involving a deceased brother and the continuation of his household when he died without the relevant offspring. The Levitical prohibitions establish the ordinary sexual and marital boundary regarding a brother’s wife.
The exceptional family duty does not erase the ordinary prohibition.
It depends upon the circumstances Scripture itself specifies.
This also helps explain something fascinating in the New Testament.
Jesus knew this law.
His opponents knew it too.
In Matthew 22, the Sadducees approached Jesus with what they thought was a devastating theological trap.
They did not believe in the resurrection.
So they constructed an extreme scenario.
A man dies childless.
His brother marries the widow.
Then that brother dies.
Another brother marries her.
He dies.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Until seven brothers have had the same woman as wife.
Then she dies.
Their question is essentially:
“Jesus, if resurrection is real, whose wife is she afterward?”
They are not primarily asking Jesus for marriage counseling.
They are trying to make resurrection look ridiculous.
But Jesus sees straight through the trap.
He tells them they are mistaken because they do not understand the Scriptures or the power of God.
The Greek wording of Matthew 22:24 reflects the levirate idea with the verb:
“ἐπιγαμβρεύσει”
epigambreusei.
In context, it refers to marrying the widow in fulfillment of this family duty.
The Sadducees know the law.
They know the technical problem.
They know the hypothetical sounds absurd.
But Jesus reveals something terrifyingly possible:
You can know a biblical rule...
and still completely misunderstand God.
You can quote Moses...
to Jesus...
and still miss the point.
Read that again.
Because that danger did not die with the Sadducees.
There are people who know verses but do not know the heart of Scripture.
People who can win theological arguments while losing tenderness.
People who can explain Hebrew and Greek while hiding secret sin.
People who defend biblical morality publicly while refusing Christ privately.
People who know enough Scripture to debate everybody...
but not enough surrender to repent.
Maybe that sentence found you.
Maybe you have been near Christianity for years.
You know the language.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know what Christians are supposed to look like.
But somewhere underneath the worship songs, Facebook posts, church attendance, theology, ministry activity, and religious vocabulary...
something is dying.
Prayer has become mechanical.
Sin has become negotiable.
Conviction has become irritating.
Jesus has become familiar.
And familiarity can become dangerous when we stop trembling at grace.
The strangest thing about levirate marriage is therefore not ultimately that an ancient Israelite could, under specific circumstances, marry his deceased brother’s widow.
The strangest thing is how easily modern readers stare at somebody else’s strange obligation while ignoring their own.
Because Christianity also confronts us with a costly call.
Not to earn salvation.
Never.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by purchasing God’s favor with religious performance.
But the grace that saves does not leave us untouched.
Jesus does not merely improve sinners.
He raises the spiritually dead.
And that brings us to the deepest distinction in this entire article.
Boaz can illustrate aspects of costly redemption.
The levirate institution can help us understand responsibility for preserving a family line.
But Jesus Christ is not merely another levirate husband.
He is infinitely greater.
We should not force every technical detail of Deuteronomy 25 into an allegory that Scripture itself does not make.
The Gospel is better than a clever analogy.
Christ redeems His people not because He was trapped by an ancient marriage statute, but because of the eternal saving purpose and love of God.
And the price was not a sandal.
It was His blood.
You and I were not merely socially vulnerable.
Scripture describes sinners as spiritually dead in trespasses and sins.
We did not simply need somebody to preserve our surname.
We needed reconciliation with God.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed righteousness we could never manufacture.
We needed resurrection.
And Jesus came.
The Son of God took flesh.
He walked into the human wreckage we created.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted hypocrites.
He ate with people religious society despised.
He carried the cross.
Nails entered His hands.
Blood ran down His body.
And the One who had no sin bore sin for sinners.
Then they buried Him.
And for a moment...
it looked like another name had been swallowed by a grave.
But Sunday came.
The stone moved.
Death lost.
Jesus rose.
And the resurrection the Sadducees mocked became the very reality proclaimed at the center of the apostolic Gospel.
That is why Christianity is not fundamentally a program for making respectable people slightly nicer.
It is news for the dead.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And sinners who repent and trust in Him can be forgiven, reconciled, redeemed, adopted, transformed, and given eternal life.
Maybe your story is scandalous.
Maybe there are chapters you desperately hope nobody reads.
Sexual sin.
Adultery.
Pornography.
Addiction.
Bitterness.
Abortion.
Pride.
A broken marriage.
A secret relationship.
Years of hypocrisy.
Years away from God.
Something you did.
Something done to you.
Something you cannot undo.
Listen carefully.
Grace does not mean your sin was insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation required the death of Christ.
But grace means your sin does not have to write the final sentence.
Jesus can.
That is repentance.
Not pretending the past never happened.
Not renaming darkness so we can remain comfortable inside it.
Repentance turns from sin toward God.
And the Gospel announces that the repentant sinner does not crawl toward a reluctant Savior.
Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
Maybe your family feels like the house in Deuteronomy 25.
A name disappearing.
A marriage collapsing.
Children wandering.
Faith dying.
Generational wounds repeating.
Everybody exhausted.
Nobody knowing how to fix what has been broken.
You may not be able to rewrite yesterday.
But yesterday does not have authority over Jesus Christ.
Bring the ruins to Him.
Bring the secret.
Bring the shame.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the resentment.
Bring the questions.
Bring the part you keep hiding behind “I’m fine.”
Stop performing.
Come into the light.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not because typing words on Facebook saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
If you are exhausted but you have not abandoned your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need believers to stand with you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”

And if Christ has already carried you through something you thought would destroy you, tell your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that ruined chapters do not have to become ruined endings.
Not as a superstition.
Not because sharing a Christian post earns favor with God.
It does not.
Send it privately to the person who stopped attending church.
And stay connected to Gospel Warrior if you want Scripture that refuses to stop at inspirational slogans and instead keeps bringing difficult questions back to Jesus Christ.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, confront sin, return to prayer, or see Christ more clearly, there is also a practical way to help sustain this work.
But understand why.
It does not make God love you more.
It does not prove that you are saved.
And nobody should ever confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Gospel itself.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.

But Christians can glorify God with their resources when they freely support faithful Gospel work, just as they can glorify Him through generosity, hospitality, service, sharing biblical truth, and countless other acts performed in faith and love.
Your support helps us keep creating, researching, writing, teaching, and sharing.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite lukewarm Christians.
Invite the person who does not even believe yet.
Not so we can build an audience around ourselves.
So we can keep pointing an audience beyond ourselves.
To Christ.
Because one day followers disappear.
Algorithms change.
Pages vanish.
Books decay.
Our names are eventually forgotten.
But Jesus remains.
And perhaps that is the final irony hidden inside this strange ancient law.
Deuteronomy speaks about preserving the name of a man who died.
The Gospel announces the Name of the Man who died...
and rose again.
Jesus.
The Name above every name.
The One no grave could erase.
The One whose kingdom cannot disappear.
The One who takes sinners with histories they cannot repair and gives them futures they could never purchase.
So yes.
Under the specific conditions given in ancient Israel’s covenant law, a man could be called to marry his deceased brother’s childless widow and fulfill the levirate responsibility.
But if that is the only fact you remember, you have missed the most important thing.
Remember the widow.
Remember the house threatened with extinction.
Remember the responsibility.
Remember the sandal.
Remember Ruth walking out of grief toward redemption.
Remember that God can move through circumstances human beings would never choose.
And above everything...
remember Jesus.
Because maybe you opened this article wondering about a dead man’s wife.
And somewhere along the way, God made you think about your own soul.
That may be the question worth answering tonight.
Not merely:
“Could he marry her?”
But:
“Have I surrendered to Christ?”
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because the most shocking thing in Scripture is not that God entered broken human stories.
It is that He still does.
Your worst chapter may explain your scars, but it does not get to name your ending when Jesus holds the pen.
